item.title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho
item.description:
Political Communication · Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho

Topics: Populism, Political communication, Election campaigns, Computational methods

When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. Drawing on the ideational approach, we operationalize populist discourse as the co-occurrence of people-centrism and anti-elitism, measured with fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers, and classify policy domains with the Comparative Agendas Project framework. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across candidates, challenging expectations that populist communication uniformly intensifies during campaigns or systematically varies across policy domains according to ideology. Rather than increasing uniformly during the campaign, populist appeals escalate strategically for some candidates as elections approach, while remaining stable for others throughout the electoral year. We propose a typology distinguishing opportunistic from consistent populists. Across policy domains, government operations serve as a baseline facilitating populist framing. Left-wing candidates increase populist rhetoric in labor/employment, consistent with issue ownership expectations, but right-wing candidates reduce populist appeals in their traditionally owned domains of law and crime and civil rights, contrary to expectations. Overall, we show that populism is neither a universal campaign imperative nor a content-neutral communication style, but a flexible discursive frame shaped by candidate strategy, electoral context, and policy content.

item.title: Skewed toward uniformity? Investigating algorithmic stereotyping and amplification in AI-generated images
item.dc:creator: Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Generative AI, Media representation, Algorithmic curation

As text-to-image generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes visual communication, concerns are growing about its role in reproducing social stereotypes. While recent algorithm auditing studies have advanced our understanding of stereotypical AI-generated imagery, they have largely focused on a narrow set of stereotypes – primarily gender and race – overlooking more nuanced forms. Addressing this gap, our study adopts a case-sensitive approach that conceptualizes stereotypes as multi-layered phenomena composed of multiple, context-specific indicators. Applying the Draw-a-Scientist Test framework, we analyzed stereotypical representations of scientists in images generated by DALL·E 3 and examined potential amplification by benchmarking against Google Images. Specifically, we compared 16 stereotype indicators across six stereotype subjects. Using Latent Class Analysis, we identified six classes reflecting distinct patterns of stereotypical depiction. Our findings show that DALL·E not only produces highly stereotypical portrayals of scientists but also amplifies these patterns compared to Google Images. Both image sources lack adequate visual references for disciplines beyond the traditional laboratory context – a pattern we interpret as epistemic narrowing, whereby diverse forms of knowledge production are reduced to a uniform, laboratory-based representation of science. We conclude by discussing potential drivers of epistemic narrowing, the broader implications of algorithmic visibility, and mitigation strategies.

item.title: From constituencies to audiences: lessons from Brazil about audience analytics in representative politics
item.dc:creator: André K. Rodarte
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · André K. Rodarte

Topics: Political communication, Audience perception, Mediatization, Social media use

The pursuit of audiences is a key driver of the mediatization of politics, yet it remains unclear how parliamentarians carry out this task. Drawing on interviews with members of Brazil’s Congress, this study investigates how politicians incorporate audience analytics into their communication strategies. It introduces a conceptual framework of audience perception – distinguishing among loyalists, followers, and audience reservoirs – to explain how politicians interpret digital publics. Findings reveal that parliamentarians’ perceptions of their audiences differ from their perceptions of electoral bases. Their follower base undergoes context collapse, disembedding audiences from their social context. Digital media re-embed these constituencies in platform contexts, wherein parliamentarians believe they must become always-on content producers, perform authenticity, and engage in information cycles. These findings reveal that audience analytics incentivize a sales orientation in parliamentary communication, distorting representation by recasting audiences as targets of influence rather than publics to whom politicians are accountable.

item.title: Immersion Matters: Virtual Reality Influences Personal and Systemic Bias Outcomes
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith
item.description:
Media Psychology · Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith

Topics: Virtual reality, Racial bias, Empathy, Media effects

Social psychological research has used traditional empathy-inducing strategies (e.g. reading, listening to, or watching narratives) to heighten recognition of and motivation to combat personal and systemic bias. We investigated whether a non-embodied 360° virtual reality (VR) experience increased recognition of and motivation to combat both personal and systemic racial bias and examined empathy as an underlying mechanism. Non-Black undergraduates in the United States (N = 313) were randomly assigned to (a) a non-embodied immersive 360° VR experience depicting racial discrimination, (b) an audio-only version of the same experience, or (c) a race-unrelated audio (control). VR exposure (vs. audio-only and control) heightened recognition of systemic bias, motivation to combat both systemic and personal bias, and perceptions of racism in isolated incidents. Emotional empathy, but not cognitive empathy, was a significant mediator. In contrast, the audio-only condition did not differ from the VR or control condition on personal and systemic bias outcomes or recognition of racism. These findings highlight the theoretical and practical value of non-embodied 360° immersive VR as a tool for combating personal and systemic bias.

item.title: Algorithmic News Selection Under News Avoidance: Assessing News Values on Chinese Tiktok (Douyin)
item.dc:creator: Jinhui Li, Wen Shi
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Jinhui Li, Wen Shi

Topics: News avoidance, Algorithmic curation, Social media algorithms, News values

This study explores how recommendation algorithms on Douyin respond to users’ growing disengagement from news by shaping the visibility of news content. Adopting an agent-based testing (ABT) approach, we conducted a 2 (intentional news avoidance: 0% vs. 100%) × 2 (unintentional news avoidance: 50% vs. 100%) between-subject experiment to simulate distinct user behaviors and capture large-scale data from news-related videos. Findings indicated that two avoidance behavioral patterns result in contrasting algorithmic outcomes which reinforce or weaken certain news values such as prominence, uniqueness, timeliness, and influence. A significant interaction effect further reveals that the influence of intentional news avoidance on the news values of influence diminishes as users’ preference for non-news content increases, whereas its influence on uniqueness becomes stronger. These findings show that recommender systems adapt to user disengagement by reprioritizing content, highlighting algorithmic curation as a socio-technical process that shapes attention amid selective news exposure.

item.title: Soft Power from the Outside, Career Choice from the Inside: Understanding Job Attractions of Chinese Media Expats in Thailand
item.dc:creator: Tucker Wang-Hai
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Tucker Wang-Hai

Topics: Journalism, Professional identity, Media systems, Journalistic practice

China’s global media expansion is often interpreted as a state-led soft power strategy. Yet little is known about how individual journalists enact this expansion while working overseas for Chinese media organizations. Taking Thailand as an empirical case, this article examines how Chinese journalists assigned to overseas postings come to view their roles as a worthwhile career decision. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Thailand and in-depth interviews with Chinese expat journalists, it argues that alignment with state goals emerges not from ideological commitment, but from personal motivations, career timing, and everyday practical reasoning. The article draws on Bourdieu’s concept of illusio to conceptualize this process as a socially grounded belief that the pursuit is worth investment. Journalists accept overseas postings insofar as these roles make sense within their own trajectories, at once professionally viable and personally meaningful. The findings complement state-centric models of media expansion and offers a framework for understanding journalists’ on-the-ground motivations amid broader transformations in global journalism.

item.title: The Many Notions of Audience Engagement: A Scoping Review
item.dc:creator: Bernadette Uth
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Bernadette Uth

Topics: Audience engagement, Journalism studies, Engaged journalism, News media

In recent years, “audience engagement” and “engaged journalism” have emerged as buzzwords in journalism studies. Audience engagement is regularly discussed as a potential remedy for declining trust in journalism and its precarious financial situation. Over the past two decades, journalism studies have thus extensively analyzed the concept, resulting in a vast body of literature on engagement. However, this has created definitional confusion around audience engagement, with numerous definitions, interpretations and characteristics of the concept discussed in existing scholarship. By conducting a systematic scoping review of 174 peer-reviewed journal articles on audience engagement, this study sheds closer light on the existing research on engagement, offers an overview on theoretical and empirical conceptualizations, and examines goals and challenges associated with engagement. The review highlights how audience engagement is examined and conceptualized in journalism scholarship, and identifies key directions for future research.

item.title: Black Lives Matter on the Ballot, in the Press: An Argument for Reporting the Long View of Contentious Solutions in Local Journalism
item.dc:creator: Brad Limov, Martin Johannes Riedl, Melissa Santillana, Sharon Strover
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Brad Limov, Martin Johannes Riedl, Melissa Santillana, Sharon Strover

Topics: Journalistic norms, Local journalism, Black Lives Matter, Solutions journalism

This paper investigates how local journalists in Austin, Texas reported on a 2021 ballot initiative mandating increased police staffing. Representing a backlash to 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, the initiative followed efforts to reallocate funds away from the Austin Police Department. Grounded in interviews with journalists who described their news choices and positionality in relation to the initiative, this case study reveals how contentious solutions to intractable social problems exacerbate tensions inherent to dominant journalistic norms. Journalists adhering to impartiality described the initiative’s underlying conflict narrowly to avoid the appearance of bias; more alarmingly, some acted as unfiltered conduits for false information by viewing coverage as a public forum for debate. We evaluate these findings against solutions-oriented journalism—an umbrella term for emerging paradigms that prioritize constructive reporting on solutions to engage news audiences in civic life—and demonstrate how these models fall short when solutions themselves are sites of intense social struggle. Inspired by journalists who resisted norms of impartiality and balance to investigate histories and trajectories of local social action, we encourage proponents of solutions-oriented journalism to prioritize rigorous, factual reporting of the long view for audiences to engage with solutions as people continuously struggle to enact them.

item.title: A privacy-preserving approach to identify riot-related footage on social media
item.dc:creator: Bryan van Horik, Naufal El Khatibi, Maurits van Galen, Lucas Spierenburg
item.description:
Computational Communication Research · Bryan van Horik, Naufal El Khatibi, Maurits van Galen, Lucas Spierenburg

Topics: Computational methods, Social media analysis, Visual communication, Machine learning

Visual social media data provides unprecedented opportunities for studying riot dynamics at fine spatiotemporal scales, yet analyzing such content raises significant privacy concerns as images can identify individuals participating in politically sensitive events. This creates tension between analytical transparency and ethical obligations that existing methods inadequately address. We propose a privacy-preserving methodology for identifying riot-related content from visual social media posts by converting images to text descriptions during data collection, then classifying these captions rather than analyzing raw visual content. Using France’s 2023 riots as a case study, we collect 107,674 Snapchat posts (19% of images, 81 % of videos) and process them through a BLIP2 image-to-text model, generating descriptive captions at a frame rate of 2 frames per second. A BERT classifier trained on 2,084 manually annotated captions achieves an F1 score of 0.73±0.03 at video-level classification, approaching the performance of direct computer vision methods (F1=0.72) while substantially enhancing privacy protection. The methodology enables researchers to share interpretable text data for replication and secondary analysis, reconciling open science principles with privacy requirements. While computational costs increase significantly (2.7B vs 5M parameters), this trade-off represents a meaningful advance for ethically studying social movements through visual social media data.

item.title: The Promise and Practice of Sharing Qualitative Data in Communication Research: Insights from the Qualitative Data Repository
item.dc:creator: Dessislava Kirilova, Lee Humphreys
item.description:
Media and Communication · Dessislava Kirilova, Lee Humphreys

Topics: Academic publishing, Research methodology, Communication research, Open science

As open science ideas gain traction in communication and media studies, qualitative researchers face unique challenges and opportunities in adopting transparent and reproducible practices. This article contributes to the growing conversation on open research infrastructures by introducing the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) as a domain-specific solution for qualitative and multi-method data sharing. QDR is particularly well-equipped to manage data derived from human participants or existing media materials, both of which are widely used in this field. We explore how QDR’s infrastructure, services, and ethical frameworks can be adapted to the needs of communication scholars. First, we briefly outline the benefits of qualitative data sharing—including increased transparency, methodological rigor, and pedagogical value—while acknowledging possible barriers such as ethical concerns, time constraints, and disciplinary histories. We then review practical developments that have taken place over the last five years by scholars practicing some of the principles for trustworthy qualitative communication research laid out by Humphreys et al. (2021). Using examples from a wide variety of projects where QDR has already facilitated data publication and annotations for transparent inquiry, we illustrate how similar practices can be adopted systematically in communication research. We also highlight QDR’s support for researchers throughout the data lifecycle, from planning and consent to curation and controlled access. This article aims to demystify qualitative data sharing and encourage broader adoption among communication and media studies scholars by showcasing QDR’s model and its alignment with findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles. We argue that embracing more open and transparent research practices not only enhances the quality and visibility of individual projects but also fosters a more inclusive and collaborative scholarly community.

item.title: African Community Media, AI, and the Question of Community Participation in the Disruptive Era
item.dc:creator: Lyton Ncube, Allen Munoriyarwa, Albert Chibuwe, Refilwe Whitney Mofokeng, Antonette Kakujaha- Murangi
item.description:
Media and Communication · Lyton Ncube, Allen Munoriyarwa, Albert Chibuwe, Refilwe Whitney Mofokeng, Antonette Kakujaha- Murangi

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Community engagement, Misinformation, Journalistic practice

In this article, we examine the nexus of Southern African community newspapers’ sceptical AI integration and grassroots democracy. The sceptical approach to AI integration in marginalised media markets of Southern African community newspapers’ news ecosystems is interrogated. We respond to the questions: In what ways is the integration of AI tools in everyday news production routines within Southern African community media institutions defined by scepticism? What is the basis of scepticism amongst Southern African community media journalists? What are the implications for grassroots democracy in these communities? The Southern African community media under study are drawn from South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled journalists and editors from these newsrooms. Findings show that the sceptical approach to AI adoption among Southern African community newspapers is largely driven by fears and concerns about AI’s documented mass production of misinformation and disinformation. In addition, the sceptical approach to AI adoption in these newsrooms is rooted in a lack of technical proficiency with AI tools and financial limitations occasioned by the decline in philanthropic funding.

item.title: Navigating Online Visibility: Construction of Feminine Identity in Chinese Influencers’ Affective Networked Publics
item.dc:creator: Qing Ma
item.description:
Media and Communication · Qing Ma

Topics: Social media influencers, Gender representation, Self-presentation, Social media platforms

The rise of fashion and beauty influencers in China has produced highly visible representations of idealised femininity that increasingly appeal to young women and girls. This study examines how influencers on the Chinese social media platform Weibo discursively construct feminine identity through digital self-branding and how young women interpret and negotiate this mediated feminine visibility. By employing in-depth interviews with 31 Chinese urban young women and a feminist critical discourse analysis of 48 selected posts produced by leading female influencers, this study identifies three interrelated discursive resources through which idealised femininity is assembled: ambiguous feminism, an entrepreneurial beauty discourse, and aspirational consumption. Drawing on Berlant’s concept of intimate publics, the study argues that these discourses circulate affectively through relatability, producing both belonging and discipline within the community. Participants actively negotiate these representations through tactically extracting symbolic values and managing pressures to construct a legible feminine subjectivity. Furthermore, this study argues that asymmetric gendered power relations are reproduced through affective circulation within feminised digital spaces.

item.title: The role of democratic values in shaping perceptions of political incivility in European liberal democracies
item.dc:creator: Sara Bentivegna, Rossella Rega
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Sara Bentivegna, Rossella Rega

Topics: Political incivility, Democratic values, Political polarization, Cross-cultural communication

This study investigates whether citizens’ perceptions of political incivility converge across liberal democracies and the extent to which individual orientations towards democracy and democratic values are associated with sensitivity to incivility. Drawing on a comparative survey conducted in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom ( N = 3500), it examines the individual factors associated with sensitivity to incivility. The results show that support for democracy and endorsement of democratic values are the most influential predictors of sensitivity to incivility, with higher levels associated with greater sensitivity, whereas anti-political attitudes are associated with lower sensitivity. These findings indicate that sensitivity to incivility is primarily associated with citizens’ orientations towards democracy and its normative principles rather than with national contextual differences. Citizens in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom assess incivility in remarkably similar ways, despite differences in electoral systems, media systems, and political cultures.

item.title: Journalistic Routines and the Social Construction of Race: A Critical Discourse Analysis of the Tyreek Hill Police Encounter
item.dc:creator: Joseph Jones
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Joseph Jones

Topics: Media framing, Journalistic practice, Discourse analysis, News coverage

To gauge U.S. journalism’s post-2020 racial reckoning, this article examines news coverage of football player Tyreek Hill’s police encounter in September 2024. Using Critical Discourse Analysis to interpret and explain digital media texts, this project mimics the contingency of the internet and considers local, national, legacy, digital-only, and sports outlets. Overall, it finds that news discourse continues to operate through a white racial frame. Even outlets that acknowledged systemic inequities or foregrounded the perspectives of the racially marginalized could recreate this dominant perspective, reinforcing tropes such as Black criminality, victim blaming, and deference to official sources. It’s thus argued that routine journalistic practices such as descriptive reporting, bothsidesism, headline conventions, reliance on official sources, and other supposedly objective norms, actually limit social discourse and the ability to have honest, good faith conversations about race. The project further highlights coverage that did counter the white racial frame and ultimately argues such coverage should be the standard. These practices are more ethical (i.e., take responsibility for the social consequences of news narratives) and provide a more nuanced and rigorous approximation of truth.

item.title: Watchdog Science Journalism: How Retraction Watch Fosters Accountability in Science
item.dc:creator: Declan Fahy
item.description:
Media and Communication · Declan Fahy

Topics: Science journalism, Academic publishing, Journalistic roles, Accountability journalism

Although science reporters have long been urged to adopt the role of the journalistic watchdog, scholars have not extensively examined how this role can be understood conceptually or in practice. This exploratory case study examines Retraction Watch, founded in 2010, as an illuminating example of watchdog science journalism that holds science to account around the epistemological claim, central to science’s cultural authority, that it is self-correcting. Drawing on a thematic analysis of interviews with senior staff at the site and scholars who study retractions, the study finds that the site has undertaken accountability journalism of the little-scrutinised phenomenon of retractions, has reported systematically on retractions, has questioned and determined the reasons for retractions, has created a database of retractions to aid science in its self-correction, and has provided knowledge-based journalism for its specialist public interested in scientific integrity. The article argues that Retraction Watch has expanded beyond journalism to operate as a novel journalistic hybrid institution that combines science journalism with the scientific infrastructure of its database, activities underpinned by a normative value of accountability. As a journalistic hybrid institution, it illustrates what future organisational forms of science journalism might look like.

item.title: Journalism as Science’s Watchdog: The Vibrancy and Vulnerability of an Increasingly Diverse Ecosystem
item.dc:creator: Alice Fleerackers, An Nguyen
item.description:
Media and Communication · Alice Fleerackers, An Nguyen

Topics: Science journalism, Research integrity, Journalistic roles, Journalism studies

Watchdog science journalism, broadly understood, investigates, exposes, and warns society of the misuses and abuses of science methods, processes, outcomes, and authority by those practicing, funding, and/or using science in the public domain. Amid rising threats to research integrity, this thematic issue provides a first comprehensive set of empirical and conceptual insights into how this type of journalism is becoming both vibrant and vulnerable. It reveals that watchdog science journalism is recognized as essential by members of the public and by journalists alike and is empowered by an increasingly diverse set of actors, both within and beyond traditional journalism. Yet, ongoing challenges within and beyond the news industry are putting pressure on this role, undermining journalists’ capacity to effectively scrutinize and sound the alarm about research integrity problems that put the public interest at risk.

item.title: From Hate Speech to Collective Action Intentions: The Role of Counter-Speech and Accuracy Cues Among Targeted Minorities
item.dc:creator: Desirée Schmuck, Magdalena Obermaier, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Muniba Saleem
item.description:
Communication Research · Desirée Schmuck, Magdalena Obermaier, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Muniba Saleem

Topics: Online hate speech, Counter-speech, Collective action, Social identity

Online hate speech targeting minority groups poses a significant social identity threat to those affected, often prompting coping strategies like out-group avoidance or derogation, which can harm intergroup relations in diverse societies. However, collective action as an empowering response has received limited attention in this context. Drawing on the social identity model of collective action (SIMCA), this study examines both the mechanisms and boundary conditions of online hate speech’s impact on minority groups. Across two experiments ( N Study1 = 328 Muslims; N Study2 = 583 Latinos), we find that online hate speech increases group-based injustice, which in turn drives collective action intentions, supporting the SIMCA. This effect is amplified when information embedded in the online hate speech is perceived as inaccurate or flagged for inaccuracy. In Study 2, we further demonstrate that counter-speech can reduce group-based injustice and, when paired with low-accuracy hate speech, enhance collective efficacy beliefs.

item.title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress
item.dc:creator: Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Oori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Oori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Mental health, Generative AI, Attachment orientation

General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

item.title: Internet Addiction Disorder and Cybersecurity Risk: A Neurobiological and Behavioral Review
item.dc:creator: Daniel Robinson, Ray Robinson
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Daniel Robinson, Ray Robinson

Topics: Internet addiction, Well-being, Digital well-being, Social engineering

Internet addiction disorder (IAD) has attracted substantial clinical and scientific interest over the past two decades. Although the condition remains outside formal diagnostic frameworks in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, accumulating neuroimaging evidence demonstrates that compulsive Internet use is associated with disruptions in dopaminergic reward circuitry and prefrontal cortical function that closely parallel those observed in substance use disorders. These neurobiological changes, encompassing impaired executive function, elevated impulsivity, and heightened reward sensitivity, may carry implications for cybersecurity. Available evidence suggests that individuals exhibiting addictive patterns of Internet use show reduced compliance with security protocols, increased vulnerability to social engineering, and elevated engagement in risky online behaviors, although directionality cannot be established with confidence given the predominantly cross-sectional evidence base. The present narrative review synthesizes evidence from addiction neuroscience, clinical psychology, and cybersecurity research to propose a mechanistic account of the IAD-cybersecurity risk relationship. The review identifies impaired prefrontal inhibitory control as the central neurobiological mediator linking IAD to cybersecurity vulnerability, mediated primarily through impulsivity and compounded by the attentional and affective characteristics that render addicted individuals susceptible to social engineering. Drawing on literature spanning 2017-2026, the review also situates this account within a contemporary regulatory context, including the documented acceleration of problematic Internet use during the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia's landmark social media minimum age legislation, and an influential 2026 civil verdict in which a U.S. jury found major platform operators liable for harms arising from addictive design. Clinical, organizational, and policy implications are discussed.

item.title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
item.dc:creator: Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim

Topics: Media addiction, Parent-child play, Executive function, Longitudinal study

Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent-child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent-child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent-child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent-child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.

item.title: The perturbing voice: Minority journalists and the struggle for journalistic legitimacy in Thailand’s Deep South
item.dc:creator: Treepon Kirdnark
item.description:
Journalism · Treepon Kirdnark

Topics: Journalistic legitimacy, Journalism, Social media, Political communication

While scholarly attention to journalistic legitimacy is growing, most studies remain concentrated in the West, overlooking the experiences of journalists in the Global South. To redress this gap, this study draws on in-depth interviews with five Muslim minority journalists in Thailand’s Deep South who actively counter Thai state narratives through social media. It examines how these journalists perform boundary work to establish legitimacy while operating amid armed conflict, securitization, and intense state surveillance. The findings identify three emerging practices that enable these minority journalists to claim the role of “partisan truth-teller”. First, they employ social media to assert cultural authority as “partisan narrators” sharing close proximity to local communities marginalized by the Thai state. Second, they use such platforms to challenge the “views” of outsiders and resist the Thai public’s widespread distrust of Malay Muslims. Finally, they confront security authorities, thereby reclaiming citizen rights and advocating for the security of Malay Muslims. In contrast to Western models of journalism as “public service”, this study contends that legitimacy in this context derives mainly from the enactment of “truth” via “partisan and perturbing voices” that defend the rights of Malay Muslim communities in Thailand.

item.title: Negotiating Professional Roles in a Constrained Media System: Role Perception and Narrated Enactment among Fact-Checkers in China
item.dc:creator: Hanye Yang
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Hanye Yang

Topics: Journalistic role theory, Fact-checking, Professional norms, Journalistic roles

This study offers the first detailed investigation into how Chinese fact-checkers perceive and narrate the enactment of professional roles within a constrained media environment. Drawing on 14 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with fact-checkers from four types of Chinese fact-checking organizations, the article provides rare qualitative evidence on a professional community that remains difficult to access. The study identifies six roles rooted in the Chinese media context: educator, rumor-buster, curator, independent advocate, gate-watcher, and facilitator. These roles show how fact-checkers negotiate professional ideals, institutional constraints, and national communication priorities in their everyday work. The article contributes to journalistic role theory by linking role perception with narrated role enactment. It shows that professional roles in constrained media systems are not simply adopted or abandoned, but situationally interpreted, negotiated, and combined. Rather than revealing a sharp divide between ideals and practice, the findings suggest a relatively strong convergence between perceived roles and narrated enactment. This convergence reflects the stability of Chinese fact-checkers’ professional self-image under institutional constraint. The article therefore demonstrates how Chinese fact-checkers articulate, justify, and normalize their professional roles, while foregrounding the symbolic and discursive processes through which perception and enactment are connected.

item.title: Optimizing Naloxone Education
item.dc:creator: Huai-yu Chen, Nicky Lewis
item.description:
Journal of Media Psychology · Huai-yu Chen, Nicky Lewis

Topics: Health communication, Message effects, Information processing, Media psychology

Abstract: Message sensation is commonly used in educational messaging to capture attention, yet its impact on cognitive learning appears paradoxical. Drawing on the Activation Model of Information Exposure and the Limited Capacity Model of Motivated Mediated Message Processing, this study examines how message sensation influences memory and knowledge improvement. An in-person 2 (death imagery: absent vs. present) × 2 (sound effects: absent vs. present) × 2 (animation: talking-head vs. action) between-subjects experiment was conducted among 603 US adults. Path modeling revealed that the need for activation moderated the effects of perceived message sensation on visual encoding and retrieval: as this need decreased, the association between perceived message sensation and memory accuracy (visual encoding and retrieval) shifted from positive to negative. These findings advance media psychology by showing how message features and individual traits interact to shape learning in high-stakes public health contexts.

item.title: Algorithmic Silences: Postcolonial Blind Spots in Dutch AI Media Discourse
item.dc:creator: Jessy de Cooker, Adája Unlandt, Jessie van Wijk
item.description:
Media and Communication · Jessy de Cooker, Adája Unlandt, Jessie van Wijk

Topics: Artificial intelligence, News coverage, Journalism studies, Media framing

The Kingdom of the Netherlands comprises four countries: the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten, as well as three public entities located on the islands of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba. All these regions are former Dutch colonies and are located in the Global South. News coverage from former colonisers toward their former colonies is shaped by historical frameworks, political interests, evolving global power dynamics, and unequal news creation. This study specifically focuses on AI coverage in European-Dutch and Caribbean-Dutch newspapers, analysing 128 articles published between 2015 and 2025. By using a structured approach to analyse AI positioning, agency attribution, political-geographical framing, and epistemic visibility, this study develops a framework for examining and understanding how news media construct narratives along colonial lines. The analysis uncovers a structural imbalance: European-Dutch media rarely engage with AI developments in the Dutch Caribbean, producing what de Sousa Santos (2015) calls a “sociology of absences,” while Caribbean outlets frequently report on European-Dutch contexts and cite Dutch policymakers, institutions, and technologies. Across both media systems, AI is predominantly described as an externally produced technology, reinforcing Northern epistemic authority and positioning the Caribbean as a recipient rather than a co-producer of AI futures. These patterns reflect structural postcolonial inequalities within the Kingdom’s media ecosystem. The study highlights the need for more inclusive and locally informed reporting on AI to ensure that technological developments and societal implications in the Dutch Caribbean are part of the wider public debate.

item.title: Media Use for Strong and Weak Ties: A Configural Examination of Personal Media System and Well-Being
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Zhang, Ronald E. Rice
item.description:
Communication Research · Xinyi Zhang, Ronald E. Rice

Topics: Well-being, Digital stress, Social networks, Media use

Taking a configural approach to personal media use, this study examined how strong- and weak-tie media configuration relate to digital stress and well-being. Using a sample of 1,197 U.S. adults (analytic N = 1,143), we explored how media configuration attributes (size, density, and centralization by tie strength, and homogeneity) are associated with well-being, directly and indirectly through five dimensions of digital stress (overconnectivity, communication overload, deficient self-regulation, self-presentation pressure, and technological frustration). Our results highlight the importance of maintaining a larger, more interconnected, and centralized weak-tie configuration, and overall, a more uniform configuration, for well-being benefits (direct and indirect). Notably, larger weak-tie configuration is indirectly associated with lower well-being through greater technological frustration, while larger strong-tie configuration is indirectly associated with higher well-being through lower technological frustration. These findings emphasize the relational context of communication media use and suggest tie-specific strategies for managing communication flows and supporting well-being.

item.title: Stratified Mobile Parenting Capital: Restrictive, Reformist and Radical Parenting Among Rural Migrant Working Families in China
item.dc:creator: Na Liu, Yutian Xiong
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Na Liu, Yutian Xiong

Topics: Mobile parenting capital, Digital inequality, Digital divide, Digital media

This study proposes the concept of mobile parenting capital, defined as the knowledge and capacities that parents draw upon to mobilise resources across spaces to support their parenting. Through interviews and observations with rural migrant worker parents, social workers and teachers in China, the study identifies three stratified parenting strategies: restrictive, reformist and radical. Restrictive parents possess limited digital resources and rely heavily on rural schools. Reformist parents actively employ digital tools to facilitate translocal parenting and support their left-behind children. Radical parents, who frequently relocate their children between rural hometowns and urban destinations, accumulate the highest levels of mobile parenting capital, while further mobilising resources from both urban and rural contexts digitally and physically.

item.title: Digital Agency Tools: A Way to Buffer the Negative Effects of Excessive Phone Use?
item.dc:creator: Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay

Topics: Smartphone use, Digital well-being, Well-being, Mobile media

In times of ubiquitous smartphone use, most users adopt one or more self-imposed rules regarding their device usage, also known as voluntary digital disconnection. Drawing on the Integrative Model of Mobile Media Use and Need Experiences (IM³UNE), this study provides empirical evidence on the adoption of digital agency tools and their potential in mitigating ill-being (depression, anxiety, and stress) associated with excessive smartphone use. We conducted a quota-based online survey involving n = 384 ( M age = 49.6) smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium). The results provide a systematization of different digital agency tools, showing they are widely used among adults. Importantly, we provide preliminary evidence on their potential in buffering ill-being due to excessive smartphone use. For users of detox apps and in-app well-being features, the associations between excessive use and ill-being were nonsignificant, unlike for nonusers of these tools. For users of default device settings, such as iOS ScreenTime, there were no differences. Our findings contribute to theory by applying and empirically testing critical elements of the IM³UNE model. Empirically, our findings indicate the importance of studying different types of tools, as they do not appear to be equally beneficial.

item.title: War or humanitarian crisis? A framing analysis of flemish media coverage of Gaza in 2023 and 2024
item.dc:creator: Gianni Blok, Ans De Nolf
item.description:
Journalism · Gianni Blok, Ans De Nolf

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Journalism, Political communication

This study analyzes how the Gaza conflict is framed in Flemish media, focusing on articles from De Standaard (DS) and Het Laatste Nieuws (HLN). Coverage was examined during three key moments over 1 year: the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, the bombings of Rafah starting May 6, 2024, and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant on November 21, 2024. Using an existing framing matrix, the study investigated (1) which frames were used, (2) how they differed between newspapers, and (3) whether they shifted across time. The results show that the human interest frame, followed by the war frame, dominated coverage in both newspapers. In the first two periods, the three most common frames were similar across DS and HLN. Only in the third period (November 2024) did the most frequently used frames differ. Over time, different framings emerged for each event, although human interest and war frames remained consistently present. Both outlets relied primarily on Western sources, leading to a potential source bias. Compared to DS, HLN presented events in a less nuanced way, which is expected from a popular newspaper. This study offers new insight into Flemish media representations of the Gaza conflict, a largely underexplored subject.

item.title: Du Boisian practice & thought for journalism studies
item.dc:creator: Tyler Leeds
item.description:
Journalism · Tyler Leeds

Topics: Journalism studies, Black press, Journalistic practice, Journalism history

W.E.B. Du Bois was a massively important 20th century journalist and intellectual. However, his journalistic practice and social theorizing are not often retrieved by journalism studies scholars as analytic resources. To make the case for his utility, I first demonstrate how Du Bois alters scholarly analyses of the 1619 Project that stress the effort’s novelty. In contrast, I situate the 1619 Project in a Du Boisian tradition marked by empiricism and positive propaganda, a combination which swims against professional journalists’ emic understandings of objectivity. I then tour moments of Du Bois’s career that show how he theorized processes of interest to journalism scholars, including his analysis of the Black press and his wider theorizing of discursive culture and its impact on habitual racism. I conclude by contrasting Du Bois to his contemporary and correspondent Walter Lippmann.

item.title: From normative principles to epistemic governance: A workflow-based analysis of European journalism ethics in datafied environments
item.dc:creator: Laurence Dierickx, Marília Gehrke, Carl‐Gustav Lindén
item.description:
Journalism · Laurence Dierickx, Marília Gehrke, Carl‐Gustav Lindén

Topics: Data journalism, Journalism ethics, Datafication, Automated journalism

Data journalism has received limited attention in journalism ethics, where it is often assumed that established normative principles apply directly to data-driven practices. However, data journalism relies on complex data processes that introduce distinct epistemic challenges related to bias, interpretation, and accountability. This study examines data journalism ethics as a form of epistemic governance embedded across key stages of the data journalism workflow, from data gathering to data visualisation, drawing on a thematic analysis of 37 ethical codes from 32 European countries. The findings show that, while ethical codes consistently articulate principles such as accuracy, fairness, and transparency, they rarely operationalise them in relation to methodological decisions shaping data-driven reporting. The epistemic governance framework serves as a bridge between data journalism ethics and AI ethics, as many AI-related ethical challenges originate in data practices and are intensified by automation.

item.title: Taking artificial intelligence from the ‘priesthood’ and providing it as a service: a media-genealogical perspective on big tech’s AI platformisation
item.dc:creator: Inga Luchs
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Inga Luchs

Topics: Platformization, Artificial intelligence, Digital platforms, Media theory

Recently, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have been positioning artificial intelligence as a utility that should be accessible to everyone. At the same time, they promote their cloud platforms as a means of ‘democratizing’ AI as they distribute easy-to-use AI services at scale. In this article, I propose a media-genealogical approach to situate this claim of ‘democratization’ within a broader development in the infrastructuralisation and platformisation of computing. I focus on three historic moments: (1) the invention of time-sharing and the idea of a ‘computer utility’ in the 1960s; (2) the introduction of abstraction to facilitate software development in the 1970s; and (3) the rise of digital platforms and the provision of user-friendly internet services in the 2000s. I demonstrate how each of these moments of ‘democratization’ is marked by a certain duality: on the one hand, they have expanded access to information technologies through the large-scale distribution of resources and the simplification of complex technologies into services. On the other hand, they have introduced new avenues for the centralisation of power. By means of a critical discourse analysis of Google’s cloud AI platform, I show how cloud companies leverage this duality to forward a process of platformisation, where they establish themselves as the central intermediaries and transform AI technologies into services to be provided at scale. This allows them to increase dependency on their infrastructures and to exert control over technological design. The media-genealogical analysis, finally, points to alternative paths that the democratisation of AI could take.

item.title: Toward a Comprehensive Understanding of Journalists’ Emotional Well-Being: Precarity, Identity and Shared Concern in Latin America
item.dc:creator: Sallie Hughes, Armando Gutiérrez Ortega, Grisel Salazar Rebolledo, Carlos Arcila Calderón, Manasvi Maheshwari, Adriana Amado, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Mireya Márquez-Ramírez, Janara Nicoletti
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Sallie Hughes, Armando Gutiérrez Ortega, Grisel Salazar Rebolledo, Carlos Arcila Calderón, Manasvi Maheshwari, Adriana Amado, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Mireya Márquez-Ramírez, Janara Nicoletti

Topics: Journalism, Well-being, Precarity, Press freedom

This study examines determinants of journalists’ emotional well-being. Drawing on stress and coping theory, role theory, and research on precarity and safety, it proposes a framework to explain concern about emotional well-being under workplace stress. Data come from the Worlds of Journalism Study in 10 Latin American countries with varying levels of press freedom. The dependent variable is a single-item report of concern about emotional well-being due to work. Hypotheses address gender, precarity, professional roles, victimization, coping, support, and press freedom. Findings show widespread concern driven by structural, organizational, and identity-based vulnerabilities. Indicators of precarity are the strongest predictors: heavier workloads increase concern, while higher income serves as a protective factor. Identity-related factors also matter: identifying as a woman and experiencing workplace bullying—reported more frequently by women—predict higher concern. Role discordance, or tension between self-censorship and professional values, further elevates concern. Unexpectedly, receiving colleague support after attacks is associated with greater concern, suggesting reactive coping or emotional contagion. Press freedom is not a significant predictor. Potential limitations include the single-item outcome and sensitivity of press freedom measures to local conditions. The study calls for organizational interventions while noting that addressing precarity requires structural changes to journalism’s financial model.

item.title: Revisiting the Indian Emergency: Collective Memory and Political Narratives in English-language Dailies
item.dc:creator: Subin Paul
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Subin Paul

Topics: Journalism studies, News coverage, Political communication, Media framing

Although the press is credited with writing the first draft of history, the relevance of the past to journalists as “purveyors of the present” remains less understood, particularly in the Global South. This article grapples with this problem by investigating the uses of the past to journalism. Building on scholarship from journalism and memory studies, I investigate the contemporary news media’s references to the Indian Emergency (1975–1977), in which the government instituted strict controls on freedom of speech and the press. Specifically, by drawing on the concept of “collective memory,” I analyze how mainstream English-language dailies constructed narratives about the Emergency during April-June 2024, a period encompassing the 2024 national election and the anniversary of the Emergency. Narrative analysis reveals two themes in coverage. First, narratives harked back to the Emergency to highlight the ruling government’s suppression of the press in contemporary India. Second, narratives projected the Emergency as a site where political debates and differences between the ruling and opposition parties were played out. This article argues that the narrative use of vernacular linguistic registers, particularly in English-language newswriting, constitutes an important feature of collective memory work and journalistic invocation of the past in this Global South context.

item.dc:creator: Michaela Šaradín Lebedíková, David Lacko, Michał Tkaczyk, Jana Blahošová, Steriani Elavsky, David Šmahel

item.title: Responsibility vs. sensationalism: A cross-cultural review of media coverage of sexual violence
item.dc:creator: Mian Ahmad Hanan, Noshina Saleem, Nasim Ishaq, Masroor Ahmed, Arooj Arshad, Imran Saeed
item.description:
Journalism · Mian Ahmad Hanan, Noshina Saleem, Nasim Ishaq, Masroor Ahmed, Arooj Arshad, Imran Saeed

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Cross-cultural communication, Media effects

In this study, the media coverage of various incidents of sexual violence across the various countries of the world has been analyzed, and to surface that whether the media is responsible, sensational or neutral in coverage of such events. Media Coverage of sexual violence is examined in the context of Galdi and Guizzo (2021), the Media-Induced Sexual Harassment (MISH) framework and Simon and Gagnon (2003) Sexual Script Theory. The review suggests that sensationalized framing and sexually objectifying representations may reinforce harmful stereotypes, reduce empathy toward survivors, and contribute to public attitudes associated with sexual violence. Through a systematic search, the data was collected from major databases from 2012 to 2021 across major academic and open-access databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, JSTOR, Web of Science, Sage Journals, and Library Genesis. Out of an initial pool of 172 potentially relevant research articles, the researchers identified and selected 135 articles that were most directly related to their specific research topic sexual violence against women for an in-depth, systematic review. The review indicates that sensational reporting remains more prevalent than responsible reporting across many cultural contexts, although important regional differences were identified.

item.title: Ten years of the mobile world congress: Media impact on the city of Barcelona
item.dc:creator: Marta Gil Ibáñez, Silvia Guillén Ruiz, Lara Martín-Vicario, Javier Bustos Díaz
item.description:
Journalism · Marta Gil Ibáñez, Silvia Guillén Ruiz, Lara Martín-Vicario, Javier Bustos Díaz

Topics: Media coverage, Sentiment analysis, Journalism, City branding

The Mobile World Congress (MWC) has become an international benchmark in mobile technology and one of the most significant events hosted in Barcelona. Beyond its technological relevance, its media visibility may have played a key role in shaping the city’s public image and international reputation. This study aims to examine the impact of media coverage of the Mobile World Congress on the promotion and positioning of the city of Barcelona. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining content analysis and sentiment analysis through the implementation of a hierarchical multiclass automatic classification system. The study analysed news coverage published in three major regional newspapers— La Vanguardia , Ara.Cat , and El Periódico ( n = 3523 news articles). This methodological design enabled the identification of thematic patterns, dominant narratives, and the frequency with which Barcelona was associated with the event. The findings indicate that media coverage of the MWC has had a notably positive effect on Barcelona’s visibility and reputation. The newspapers consistently presented the city as a leading hub for technological innovation, international business, and large-scale global events. Recurrent references to Barcelona’s organisational capacity and strategic relevance within the mobile technology sector contributed to strengthening its urban brand and enhancing its symbolic capital in both regional and international media discourse. The MWC has significantly contributed to boosting and promoting the city of Barcelona. Media representation of the event has reinforced the city’s status as a global, innovation-driven urban centre and has consolidated its position within the international technological landscape.

item.title: Involuntarily mediatized third place: sustaining cultural practices in China’s post-industrial communities
item.dc:creator: Xin Wenjuan
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Xin Wenjuan

Topics: Mediatization, Digital media, Social media platforms, Digital inequality

Abstract Drawing on third place and mediatization theories, this study examines how cultural practices are reorganized under infrastructural withdrawal in post-industrial China. Through ethnographic fieldwork with a Qinqiang opera troupe in a former danwei mining settlement, it analyzes how the erosion of physical venues and institutional support transforms collective participation. Findings show that cultural practices are reorganized through fragmented digital arrangements—WeChat coordination, platform visibility, livestream interaction, and temporary hybrid spaces. Rather than voluntary adoption, this constitutes involuntary mediatization, where mediation becomes structurally necessary when offline alternatives vanish. The study conceptualizes this as the involuntarily mediatized third place, extending third place theory by showing how sociability reconstitutes through distributed socio-technical infrastructures under withdrawal. It argues that cultural continuity persists not through institutional reproduction, but through fragile, intergenerationally distributed mediation shaped by platform logics and infrastructural dependency.

item.title: Predicting Irritation Disclosures in Romantic Relationships: Testing and Extending the Revelation Risk Model
item.dc:creator: Rudy C. Pett, Anita L. Vangelisti
item.description:
Communication Research · Rudy C. Pett, Anita L. Vangelisti

Topics: Self-disclosure, Interpersonal communication, Relationship power, Longitudinal study

Feelings of irritation often emerge in romantic relationships. However, the theoretical mechanisms predicting whether individuals disclose these feelings to their romantic partner remain limited and largely reliant on examining indicators of future behavior rather than actual future behavior. Using a two-month, longitudinal survey design involving 448 participants, the current study tested the Revelation Risk Model (RRM) as a mechanism for predicting whether individuals would disclose or conceal feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power was also incorporated as an additional predictor. The original RRM components (i.e., closeness, risk, communication efficacy, willingness to disclose) collectively predicted whether individuals disclosed or concealed feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power predicted individuals’ communication efficacy, as well as perceived risk associated with disclosing their feelings of irritation. The findings are discussed in terms of their contributions to existing research on disclosure, irritations, and power in romantic relationships.

item.title: mlstats : An R Package for Multilevel Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation
item.dc:creator: Felix Dietrich
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Felix Dietrich

Topics: Research methodology, Computational methods, Measurement validity, Mobile communication

Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats , an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics—including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations—in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on Comprehensive R Archive Network with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/ .
